description: Software that a usage heuristic must never flag as unused. See Data/README.md, section 'unused-app-exclusions.json'. Curated by hand; every entry states why. Over-matching here costs a missed finding, which is the safe direction.

entries.reason: A redistributable runtime, not an application. Nobody launches it, so any usage heuristic reads it as unused; removing one breaks every program compiled against it. This machine carries 24 such entries.
Runtime and shared framework, never launched directly. Removing one takes every .NET application on the machine with it.
The embedded browser runtime a large number of desktop applications render their UI with. It has no window of its own and is never launched by a user.
Input runtime installed by games. No UI, never launched; removing it costs controller support in whatever installed it.
Graphics runtime installed by games and drivers. Never launched by a user.
Physics runtime installed alongside the graphics driver. No UI; games load it, users do not.
Prerequisite runtime bundles written by game launchers (Epic and friends). They exist only to satisfy a dependency and are never launched.
A runtime plus its background updater. Java applications launch it; users do not, so a usage heuristic sees it as untouched however much Java code runs.

entries.displayName: Python interpreter and its install components
entries.reason: A Python install registers one entry per component (core interpreter, standard library, pip bootstrap, Tcl/Tk, test suite, documentation). None of them is a launchable application, and this machine carries eleven of them for one Python.

entries.displayName: NVIDIA driver, driver components and driver-update utility
entries.reason: Every NVIDIA-published uninstall entry on a Windows machine is the graphics driver, one of its containers/services/plugins, or the app that updates it. This machine carries twenty of them, none user-launched. Removing one costs the display driver or its update path.

entries.displayName: AMD chipset, CPU and platform drivers
entries.reason: AMD-published uninstall entries are chipset, GPIO, PSP, SMBus and power-management drivers plus their installers. Eleven on this machine, none of them launchable.
Chipset, management-engine and platform drivers. Not applications; removing one can cost the machine a bus or a power feature.
entries.note: The Store package names here come from published lists and have not been seen on this project's hardware; this machine is AMD. A wrong identifier in an exclusion list costs nothing -- it matches nothing.

entries.reason: Audio and Ethernet drivers. Never launched; removing one costs sound or the network adapter.

Hardware abstraction layers for RGB, capture and storage peripherals, installed by the peripheral's software. Ten entries on this machine across three spellings of the same publisher, none of them a program a user opens.

These update firmware and drivers. Treating one as bloat because nobody opens it is how a machine loses its fan curve or its BIOS-update path. Named in Data/README.md as software that must never be flagged.
entries.note: 9426MICRO-STARINTERNATION.MSICenter was measured on this project's hardware and is why the Store half of this entry exists: MSI Center ships as an Appx package, so the registryDisplayName patterns alone missed it and it came out as a candidate Finding. The Lenovo/Dell/HP/ASUS Store identifiers come from published lists and are unverified here.

entries.displayName: Peripheral and storage device control software
entries.reason: Device control services and dashboards for keyboards, mice, coolers and drives. They run as background services with no window a user opens, and they carry the firmware-update path for the device.

Security software is never flagged as unused, full stop (docs/STATE.md). It is deliberately invisible in normal use, so a usage heuristic sees every one of these as untouched. The security-trial carve-out that lets the OEM whitelist name a trial edition does NOT extend to this detector.
entries.note: Malwarebytes.AntiMalware was measured on this project's hardware as a Store package, which the registryDisplayName patterns alone would have missed.

entries.reason: Kernel-level anti-cheat installed by games. It has no user-facing window at all, so it reads as never used no matter how much the game is played, and removing it stops the game from launching.

A VPN client is security software the user chose, and it spends most of its life as a background service and a tray icon rather than a window. Flagging one as unused is both wrong and the kind of wrong that discredits the tool.

entries.displayName: Windows shell and OS component packages
entries.reason: Shell, sign-in, settings and system-UI packages. Most are never launched from a Start-menu tile at all, and removing one costs a piece of Windows itself.
Framework packages other packages depend on (VCLibs, .NET Native, WinUI, WebView2, the app runtime). They have no entry point to launch, so no usage signal can ever exist for them.
The Store is how the user reinstalls anything this tool removes, and App Installer is the winget host. Both are named in Data/README.md as never-removable.
A sync client does its job with no window open. It reads as unused precisely when it is working, and removing one can strand the only local copy of the user's files.

entries.displayName: Background services, agents and updater helpers
entries.reason: Services, online-service backends and certificate/update helpers shipped alongside an application. They have no UI, so absence of usage evidence says nothing about them, and they are removed by uninstalling their parent rather than on their own.
